extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in humor, linguistics, and wordplay (general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify the type of pun and evaluate its effectiveness according to formal properties (mechanism, simultaneous meanings, insight, precision, and fit). Useful for analysis, creation, or critique of puns in writing or cartoons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: polysemy/homonymy/phonological similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns involve polysemy, homonymy, or phonological similarity to another word, for an intended humorous or rhetorical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanism of word relation (polysemy, homonymy, sound similarity) is the defining property; a working evaluation should check which of these is at play and whether it is used intentionally for humor or rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homophonic puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Words sound the same but are spelled differently with different meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Atheism is a non-prophet institution.' Evaluate whether two words truly share sound, differ in spelling/meaning, and whether the sound-alike mapping produces a meaningful second script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homographic puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Words spelled the same but pronounced differently and have different meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.' Check that spelling identity supports two pronunciations/meanings and that both meanings are relevant to the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homonymic puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Same spelling AND same sound, different meanings (combines homograph and homophone properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.' Verify that the identical form legitimately supports two distinct senses (e.g., verb vs noun) used in parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple puns occur in the same sentence or utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Why do we still have troops in Germany? To keep the Russians in Czech.' Evaluate density: multiple distinct punful mappings can increase cleverness but risk forcedness or overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive puns
rubrics_metrics.description: The second part of the utterance requires understanding the first for the pun to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A Freudian slip is when you say one thing but mean your mother.' Judge whether the dependency is clear and whether recursion produces an extra comedic payoff rather than confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Image-based wordplay (punning through visual depiction rather than purely linguistic forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in cartoons and graphic media (e.g., New Yorker). Evaluate whether the image simultaneously activates multiple readings and whether visual elements align precisely with the alternate script.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bilingual puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns that use words from two different languages to create a double reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience language knowledge requirements and whether cross-linguistic similarity is exploited clearly and fairly given the intended readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script opposition / simultaneous activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two scripts are activated simultaneously (script opposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful pun typically triggers two competing scripts; evaluation should check that both scripts are plausible and available to the audience so the dual reading occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader recognition / 'Aha' moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader recognizes the dual meaning; an 'aha' moment of seeing the linkage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectiveness depends on the audience perceiving both readings and experiencing the moment of linkage. If the dual meaning is missed, the pun fails; if it's too immediate, it may feel trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insight versus mere match
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the dual meaning illuminate something (insight) or just match (groan)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the pun offers additional perspective or commentary beyond the wordplay itself. Puns that illuminate tend to be judged funnier/cleverer than those that only produce a word match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection precision versus strained link
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the connection between meanings precise or strained?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise, well-motivated connections improve comedic effect; strained or forced links make puns groan-worthy. Rate how naturally the alternate reading follows from the context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic fit into sentence/context
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the pun fit organically into the sentence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pun that arises naturally from context is stronger than one awkwardly inserted. Check syntactic and semantic integration with surrounding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too obvious or forced (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns that are too obvious or feel forced tend to be groan-worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark as a negative quality: if the joke's dual reading is telegraphed without surprise or feels contrived, it is likely to elicit groans rather than laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun is the only payoff (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the pun is the sole payoff with no additional insight, it often falls flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the pun is supported by narrative, characterization, or additional wit; solitary, surface-level puns are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun-groan as ritual response (meta-observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'groan' reaction to a pun can itself be a ritualized response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note as a sociolinguistic phenomenon: groaning may signal communal recognition rather than objective failure; consider audience norms when judging success.
